slides.title: Title
slides.notes: Open by framing the section as a pipeline rather than a list of definitions. A bifunction packages perturbations of a primal problem, and the adjoint packages the dual problem that reads those perturbations as certificates. The lecture keeps three diagnostics visible: weak duality, normality, and the saddle point certificate.

slides.title: Perturbation Model
slides.notes: Before introducing the adjoint, make sure the primal object is concrete. A bifunction is a family of objective functions indexed by a perturbation. The value function takes each perturbation and returns the best primal value. The geometric role of a multiplier is to provide a supporting slope to that value function at zero.

slides.title: Concave Mirror
slides.notes: This slide sets up the sign discipline. The same convex analysis vocabulary has a concave counterpart: infimum becomes supremum, lower semicontinuity becomes upper semicontinuity, and supporting lower affine functions become supporting upper affine functions. That is why the adjoint dual program is naturally a maximization problem.

slides.title: Adjoint Definition
slides.notes: Introduce the formula as a graph-function conjugacy with a sign convention. The infimum subtracts the dual pairing with the primal variable and adds the pairing with the perturbation. The output is no longer a convex bifunction in the same direction; it is a concave bifunction whose variables are the dual coordinates.

slides.title: Involution
slides.notes: The adjoint is not merely a way to manufacture a new function; it is an involutive correspondence after closure. If the original bifunction has no missing boundary points, the second adjoint gives the same object back. This is the structural reason the dual of the dual can be identified with the original program.

slides.title: Linear Transpose
slides.notes: Use the linear example to make the abstraction feel earned. If the bifunction only records the graph of a linear map, the adjoint records the graph of the transpose map. The general construction keeps that same geometry, but it allows convex relations and objective terms instead of only exact linear equations.

slides.title: Dual Program
slides.notes: This is the point where the adjoint becomes an optimization problem. The primal optimizes the zero perturbation slice of F, while the dual optimizes the zero perturbation slice of F-star. Perturbations also swap: primal perturbations live in u, and dual perturbations live in x-star.

slides.title: Weak Duality
slides.notes: Connect the theorem to the visual invariant in the notebook. Every dual feasible value is a valid lower bound for every primal feasible value, so the dual curve sits below the primal curve. The remaining question is whether the two curves meet at the unperturbed problem or leave a positive gap.

slides.title: Normality
slides.notes: Normality is the section's central stability condition. It says that the value at the original problem is the limit predicted by nearby perturbations. When this closure condition holds, the dual lower bound reaches the primal value. When it fails, the gap is a real discontinuity in the perturbation model.

slides.title: Kuhn-Tucker
slides.notes: The theorem identifies two things that can look unrelated. A Kuhn-Tucker vector is a sensitivity certificate for the primal perturbation function, while a dual optimal solution maximizes the adjoint objective. Normality lets the subgradient certificate pass through conjugacy and become an optimizer on the dual side.

slides.title: Saddle Certificate
slides.notes: Read the saddle inequality in the correct directions. Holding the primal point fixed, the chosen dual variable is best for the maximization side. Holding the dual variable fixed, the chosen primal point is best for the minimization side. This single saddle picture explains why an apparent reverse inequality between candidate values closes the duality gap.

slides.title: Ordinary Programs
slides.notes: Close the abstract theory back onto the familiar constrained problem. For inequality constraints, nonnegative multipliers form lower bounds through the Lagrangian. Rockafellar's bifunction language explains why the familiar dual is sometimes only the visible part of a richer perturbation model, especially when nonlinear constraints need translations as well as right-hand-side shifts.

slides.title: Notebook Lab
slides.notes: Tie the lecture back to the assigned notebook. The artifact is a test bench for weak duality: primal values should never fall below their paired dual bounds. Students should treat changes to perturbations or multipliers as experiments on the certificate. If the inequality fails, the setup no longer matches the hypotheses or the sign convention.

slides.title: Recap
slides.notes: End with a working checklist. Start with a perturbation model, read dual variables as supporting slopes, build the adjoint program, and use weak duality as the baseline inequality. Equality then comes from normality or from a saddle point certificate that simultaneously proves primal and dual optimality.
